pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Cucumber mosaic, caused by the cucumber mosaic virus (abbreviated as CMV) is a worldwide, highly infectious viral disease

type_of_disease.quote: Cucumber mosaic, caused by the cucumber mosaic virus (abbreviated as CMV) is a worldwide, highly infectious viral disease

affected_parts.quote: Symptoms associated with CMV infections: stunting mosaic pattern of light and dark green (or yellow and green) on the leaves. malformation of leaves or growing points yellow streaking of leaves (especially monocots) yellow spotting on leaves ring-spots or line patterns on leaves or fruit flower color breaking distinct yellowing only of veins. The virus particles are found in all parts of the plant except the few cells at the tips of the growing points.

summary.value: CMV causes stunting, mosaic patterns of light and dark green or yellow and green on leaves, malformation of leaves and growing points, yellow streaking and spotting, ring-spots or line patterns on leaves or fruit, flower color breaking, and yellowing of veins.
summary.quote: Symptoms associated with CMV infections: stunting mosaic pattern of light and dark green (or yellow and green) on the leaves. malformation of leaves or growing points yellow streaking of leaves (especially monocots) yellow spotting on leaves ring-spots or line patterns on leaves or fruit flower color breaking distinct yellowing only of veins

diagnostic_features.value: Alternating light and dark green mosaic pattern on leaves, especially younger leaves, with possible shoestring-like appearance of leaves; plants appear lighter in color, bushy and stunted.
diagnostic_features.quote: a mosaic (alternating light and dark green areas) on at least some leaves, especially on the younger leaves. Leaves may exhibit a shoestring-like appearance.

look_alikes.quote: These symptoms can be confused with those caused by tobacco mosaic virus

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Early blight, caused by the fungus Alternaria solani

type_of_disease.quote: caused by the fungus Alternaria solani

diagnostic_features.value: Lesions are larger and darker brown than Septoria leaf spots and display concentric rings.
diagnostic_features.quote: Lesions caused by the early blight pathogen will be larger and darker brown than Septoria leaf spots and will have concentric rings.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Botrytis gray mold is caused by the ubiquitous asexual fungus Botrytis cinerea (B. cinerea)

type_of_disease.quote: caused by the ubiquitous asexual fungus Botrytis cinerea

affected_parts.quote: Botrytis can affect all aboveground plant parts of tomato in both the greenhouse and field. This fungus occurs as both a pathogen and a saprophyte causing diseases such as damping off, stem girdling, foliar blighting, and postharvest rots.

summary.value: Botrytis produces a dense velvety gray-brown spore mass on infected tissue. Lesions on leaves and stems are tan to brown in color. In high humidity, fluffy gray spores cover infected plant parts. Fruit lesions appear as a whitish soft rot with characteristic small white rings (ghost spots) of 3–8 mm on the fruit surface representing aborted infections.
summary.quote: Botrytis produces a dense velvety gray brown spore mass on infected tissue which when disturbed releases a cloud of spores. Tomato leaf and stem lesions are tan to brown in color. Fruit lesions are typically a whitish soft rot and often the skin ruptures near the center of the decayed area allowing spores to form on exposed tissue. Small 3-8 mm whitish rings on the fruit surface are aborted botrytis infections known as ghost spots which reduce market quality.

diagnostic_features.value: Dense velvety gray-brown spore mass that releases a cloud of spores when disturbed; stem lesions may expand in concentric rings to girdle the entire stem causing wilting above the infection site; spores are light brown-gray on black stalks; characteristic 3–8 mm whitish ghost spot rings on fruit surface; leaves show irregular to V-shaped brown blotches often starting at margins.
diagnostic_features.quote: Botrytis produces a dense velvety gray brown spore mass on infected tissue which when disturbed releases a cloud of spores. Stem lesions may expand in concentric rings to girdle the entire stem causing wilting above the infection site. Small 3-8 mm whitish rings on the fruit surface are aborted botrytis infections known as ghost spots which reduce market quality.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Tomato late blight is caused by the oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans ( P. infestans )

affected_parts.quote: Symptoms of late blight may be found on any above-ground part of the tomato plant. Infected leaves typically have... Stem and petiole lesions are brown... Discoloration may also occur on the flowers, causing them to drop. Symptomatic tomato fruits appear mottled...

summary.value: Infected leaves develop green to brown patches of dead tissue surrounded by a pale green or gray border; under humid and wet conditions, lesions appear water-soaked, dark brown, and greasy, with white fuzzy growth on undersides of leaves and lower stems. Stem and petiole lesions are brown and not well-defined in shape. Flowers may discolor and drop. Fruit lesions appear as firm, greasy spots that become leathery and chocolate brown, or mottled with golden to dark brown firm sunken surfaces with associated white fuzzy pathogen growth.
summary.quote: Infected leaves typically have green to brown patches of dead tissue surrounded by a pale green or gray border. When the weather is very humid and wet, late blight infections can appear water-soaked or dark brown in color, and are often described as appearing greasy. White, fuzzy growth may be found on the undersides of leaves or on lower stems. Stem and petiole lesions are brown and are typically not well defined in shape. Discoloration may also occur on the flowers, causing them to drop. Symptomatic tomato fruits appear mottled, often with golden to dark brown, firm, sunken surfaces. White, fuzzy pathogen growth can also be found in association with the fruit lesions.

diagnostic_features.value: White fuzzy pathogen sporulation visible on undersides of leaves and lower stems; lesions are brown and papery with rings of white fuzzy sporulation; leaf lesions surrounded by distinctive pale green or gray halos; water-soaked or greasy appearance under humid conditions; late blight lesions found anywhere on plant (especially new growth) and are light brown or tan, distinguishing them from early blight (dark brown with concentric rings, starting on lower leaves).
diagnostic_features.quote: White, fuzzy growth may be found on the undersides of leaves or on lower stems. Lesions are brown and papery with rings of white, fuzzy pathogen sporulation. Infected leaves typically have green to brown patches of dead tissue surrounded by a pale green or gray border. When the weather is very humid and wet, late blight infections can appear water-soaked or dark brown in color, and are often described as appearing greasy.

look_alikes.quote: Other species of Phytophthora, specifically P. nicotianae and P. capsici, can also cause lesions on tomato and tomato fruit similar to those caused by late blight; Late blight can be differentiated from early blight on tomato and other foliar fungal diseases

conflicts.note: UMN Extension describes Phytophthora infestans as 'a water mold' but does not explicitly use the term 'oomycete' for disease type classification.

conflicts.canonical_value: Infected leaves develop green to brown patches with pale green or gray border; white fuzzy growth on undersides; stem lesions brown; fruit mottled with firm sunken golden to dark brown surfaces (UW Vegetable Pathology)
conflicts.alternative_value: Large dark brown blotches with gray-green edges on leaves; infected fruit have a dry brown rot
conflicts.note: UMN Extension describes leaf lesions as 'large brown blotches with a green gray edge' and fruit as having 'a dry brown rot', while NC State and UW describe fruit as greasy/leathery and leaf lesions as having pale green or gray halos.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Bacterial canker is caused by Clavibacter michiganensis subsp. michiganensis (Cmm).

type_of_disease.quote: Bacterial canker is one of the most devastating bacterial pathogens of tomato worldwide.

affected_parts.quote: Cmm infections result in wilting, defoliation, desiccation, skin cankers, significantly reduced fruit yield and quality... greenhouse-grown tomatoes will frequently have scorching or browning on the margins of leaflets... may have cankers forming on the stems... bird-eye lesions on the fruit

summary.value: Symptoms include wilting, defoliation, and desiccation of leaves, along with brown canker lesions on stems and fruit marked by characteristic dark spots surrounded by white halos.
summary.quote: Cmm infections result in wilting, defoliation, desiccation, skin cankers, significantly reduced fruit yield and quality, and ultimately plant death.

diagnostic_features.value: The bird-eye spots on the fruit are small dark brown lesions that are surrounded by a white halo and may become raised as symptoms progress, with scorching and browning of leaf margins. Bacterial canker can be distinguished from bacterial speck by excessive wilting, canker development, and prominent bird's-eye spots on fruit.
diagnostic_features.quote: The bird-eye spots on the fruit are small dark brown lesions that are surrounded by a white halo and may become raised as the symptoms progress... Tomato leaves that contain scorching and browning with distinctive 'bird-eye' lesions on the fruit

look_alikes.quote: Bacterial speck causes similar symptoms to bacterial spot and canker of tomato. However, discrete differences can allow for the accurate diagnosis of the pathogen.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Bacterial speck of tomato is caused by the bacterium Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato

type_of_disease.quote: caused by the bacterium Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato

affected_parts.quote: Bacterial speck produces small (1/16 in.) slightly-raised black 'speck-like' lesions on the developing fruit that are much smaller than tomatoes with bacterial spot. On tomato leaves, similar lesions to bacterial spot appear except that faint yellow halos surround the lesions and the leaf may show substantial curling.

summary.value: Small black spots with yellow halos on leaves and fruit. On leaves, spots are 1/8 to 1/4 inch in diameter, angular, and more prominent on undersides; on fruit, spots are pinpoint-like, slightly raised, and can be raised, flat, or sunken, ranging from brown to black.
summary.quote: Small black spots (approximately ⅛ to ¼ inch in diameter) that often are more prominent on the undersides of leaves. As the spots age, a yellow halo may develop around the edge. Spots on fruit are very small (almost pinpoint-like) and do not penetrate very deeply into the tissue. The spots can be raised, flat or sunken, and range in color from brown to black.

diagnostic_features.value: Small (1/16 in.) slightly-raised black speck-like lesions on developing fruit much smaller than those of bacterial spot; on leaves, small angular (straight-edged) spots with yellow halos; substantial leaf curling may also be present.
diagnostic_features.quote: Bacterial speck produces small (1/16 in.) slightly-raised black 'speck-like' lesions on the developing fruit that are much smaller than tomatoes with bacterial spot. On tomato leaves, similar lesions to bacterial spot appear except that faint yellow halos surround the lesions and the leaf may show substantial curling.

look_alikes.quote: Bacterial spot, (see UW Plant Disease Facts D0012, Bacterial Spot of Tomato) and tomato spotted wilt (a viral disease) may cause similar leaf symptoms.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: caused by the soil-borne bacterium Ralstonia solanacearum Race 1

type_of_disease.quote: caused by the soil-borne bacterium Ralstonia solanacearum Race 1

affected_parts.quote: The pathogen enters plant roots through small wounds... The bacteria then multiply in the vascular system... the base of the plant may show brown cankers, root rot, and a section of an infected stem may show a brown discoloration of the vascular tissue... The plant eventually becomes permanently wilted and death occurs.

summary.value: Initially, infected plants develop wilt symptoms in the afternoon and recover in the evening. As the disease progresses, the base of the plant shows brown cankers and root rot with vascular discoloration, eventually leading to permanent wilt and plant death.
summary.quote: Initially, infected plants develop wilt symptoms in the afternoon, and recover in the evening... the base of the plant may show brown cankers, root rot, and a section of an infected stem may show a brown discoloration of the vascular tissue (fig. 1). The plant eventually becomes permanently wilted and death occurs.

diagnostic_features.value: A white slimy bacterial substance streams from a freshly cut stem base placed in water, which is a strong indicator of bacteria in the vascular tissue. The interior stem shows dark or light brown discoloration in the pith area.
diagnostic_features.quote: A freshly cut stem at the base of the plant placed in water can show a stream of a white slimy substance (fig. 2A) that is a strong indicator of the bacterium present in the vascular tissue (fig. 2B). The interior of the stem also can be a dark or light brown in the pith area (fig. 3).

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: TSWV is a member of the genus, Orthotospovirus—a group of plant viruses

type_of_disease.quote: TSWV is a member of the genus, Orthotospovirus—a group of plant viruses

affected_parts.quote: On tomatoes infected with TSWV, the uppermost leaves appear bronzed with small brown lesions... Infected foliage on both tomatoes and peppers may become covered with so many spots that the entire leaf browns, rolls, and wilts. Symptoms on the fruit of both tomatoes and peppers typically include yellow ringspots and brown necrotic sunken areas

summary.value: Infected leaves appear bronzed with small brown lesions or necrotic spots; infected foliage may become covered with so many spots that leaves brown, roll, and wilt. Fruit develops yellow ringspots and brown necrotic sunken areas. Young leaves develop bronzing on upper surfaces followed by distinct necrotic spots, with leaves cupping downward and tip dieback. Ripe fruit shows chlorotic spots and blotches with concentric rings; green fruit shows slightly raised areas with faint concentric zones.
summary.quote: Plants infected with Tomato spotted wilt virus exhibit bronzing of the upper sides of young leaves, which later develop distinct, necrotic spots. Leaves may be cupped downward. Some tip dieback may occur. On ripe fruit chlorotic spots and blotches appear, often with concentric rings. Green fruit show slightly raised areas with faint, concentric zones.

diagnostic_features.value: Lesions caused by TSWV have blurred margins, whereas lesions from other diseases have definite margins. Bronzing on upper leaf surfaces, distinct necrotic spots, downward-cupped leaves, tip dieback, and concentric ring patterns on ripe fruit or raised zones on green fruit are key diagnostic features.
diagnostic_features.quote: lesions caused by TSWV have blurred margins, while the margins of lesions caused by other diseases are definite

look_alikes.quote: Symptoms of TSWV may also resemble symptoms of early blight or other leaf spot diseases... Symptoms of TSWV can be variable and some are similar to symptoms of other viruses

conflicts.note: USU Extension lists seeds and pods as affected parts; NC State and UC IPM do not mention seeds or pods for tomato specifically
USU Extension describes TSWV as a Tospovirus; NC State notes the genus is Orthotospovirus (updated taxonomy). Both agree it is viral.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Alternaria stem canker is caused by the pathogen Alternaria alternata f. sp. lycopersici (= Clathrospora diplospora ).

type_of_disease.quote: Collar rot and Alternaria stem canker of tomato are both caused by fungal pathogens in the genus Alternaria.

affected_parts.quote: Symptoms of Alternaria stem canker can appear on the stems, leaves, and fruit of tomato plants. Vascular and pith tissue directly above and below the cankers may have brown streaks and become cracked and dry.

summary.value: Alternaria stem canker is characterized by large, irregularly shaped, dark-brown to almost black cankers with light and dark concentric rings on stems near the soil line, enlarging to cause girdled stems, stem death, and plant collapse.
summary.quote: Alternaria stem canker is characterized by the formation of large, irregularly shaped, dark-brown to almost black cankers with light and dark concentric rings on stems near the soil line. Cankers will enlarge as the plant grows causing girdled stems, stem death, and plant collapse.

diagnostic_features.value: Alternaria stem canker causes large, irregularly shaped stem lesions with pronounced concentric rings. Vascular and pith tissue directly above and below cankers develop brown streaks and become cracked and dry. Spores are formed in chains of 3-5, light olive brown to dark brown, hand grenade-shaped with a shorter beaked apical cell on the terminal end, and are 7-18 x 18-50 µm in size.
diagnostic_features.quote: Causes large, irregularly shaped stem lesions with pronounced concentric rings. Vascular and pith tissue directly above and below the cankers may have brown streaks and become cracked and dry. conidia of A. alternata f. sp. lycopersici are formed in chains, light olive brown to dark brown, "hand grenade" shaped, have three to five cross septa with longitudinal septa in the second and third cells, and a shorter, beaked apical cell on the terminal end. Conidia are 7-18 x 18-50 µm in size.

look_alikes.quote: Both pathogens can cause large, irregularly shaped stem lesions with pronounced concentric rings.

conflicts.note: Texas A&M source lists only Foliar and Stem; NC State source additionally identifies vascular tissue involvement.

conflicts.canonical_value: Large, irregularly shaped, dark-brown to almost black cankers with light and dark concentric rings on stems near the soil line, enlarging to cause girdled stems, stem death, and plant collapse.
conflicts.alternative_value: Large dark brown cankers form on stems; cankers may dry and split. These cankers will girdle the stem as they enlarge, killing the entire plant.
conflicts.note: Texas A&M description is less detailed; NC State preferred as higher-authority extension source.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: caused by several species of the fungus Colletotrichum, (Colletotrichum coccodes is the most common)

type_of_disease.quote: Tomato anthracnose (ripe rot) is a fungal disease

affected_parts.quote: Fruit: Initially small, circular, water-soaked spots that are slightly sunken will appear on over ripened tomatoes. Leaves and Stems: small, dark spots with yellow halos may appear on older leaves, and tiny lesions may occur on stems. Roots: Less commonly identified are root infections.

summary.value: Anthracnose initially appears as small, circular, water-soaked and sunken spots on overripe tomatoes. These lesions form concentric rings, expand to ½" in diameter, darken progressively, and may merge to cause complete fruit decay. Leaf symptoms appear as small, dark spots surrounded by a yellow halo on older leaves. During damp weather, masses of salmon-colored spores may develop on lesion surfaces.
summary.quote: Initially small, circular, water-soaked spots that are slightly sunken will appear on over ripened tomatoes. These lesions can form concentric rings and expand up to ½" in diameter while also getting deeper and darker. Individual lesions can group together resulting in a large rotting area and ultimately complete fruit decay.

diagnostic_features.value: Dark fungal structures visible in the center of spots; salmon pink spore appearance under humid conditions; concentric ring pattern with tan center and dark specks; water-soaked and sunken lesions expanding to approximately ½" in diameter.
diagnostic_features.quote: The center of anthracnose spots becomes dark as the fungus produces spores. Looking toward the center of the spots, dark fungal structures may be seen, or if conditions remain very humid, the spores will have a salmon pink appearance to them. These lesions can form concentric rings and expand up to ½" in diameter.

look_alikes.quote: Not to be Confused with: Blossom End Rot - Water-soaked lesions, usually form on the lower side of the tomato fruit Late Blight - Sunken spots on tomato fruit are less circular in appearance

conflicts.note: WSU source mentions only leaf and fruit involvement; UConn source is more comprehensive listing leaves, stems, roots, and fruit.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Leaf mold is caused by the fungus Passalora fulva (previously called Fulvia fulva or Cladosporium fulvum)

type_of_disease.quote: Leaf mold is caused by the fungus Passalora fulva

affected_parts.quote: Foliage is often the only part of the plant directly infected... In severe cases, blossoms and fruit can also be infected

summary.value: Pale greenish-yellow spots on the upper leaf surface with olive-green to brown velvety mold on the lower surface. Infected leaves eventually wither and die. Fruit infections appear as smooth black irregular areas on the stem end.
summary.quote: Pale greenish-yellow spots, usually less than 1/4 inch, with no definite margins, form on the upper sides of leaves. Olive-green to brown velvety mold forms on the lower leaf surface below leaf spots. Leaves wither and die but often remain attached to the plant. Fruit infections start as a smooth black irregular area on the stem end of the fruit.

diagnostic_features.value: Discrete yellow spots on upper leaf surface with corresponding olive spores on underside; oldest leaves infected first; velvety mold texture on lower leaf surface; spots typically less than 1/4 inch with no definite margins. Lesions appear as brighter yellow with indistinct chlorosis on upper leaf surface, underside shows olive-green fuzzy fungal growth.
diagnostic_features.quote: Discrete yellow spots on the upper side of the leaf and the corresponding olive spores on the underside. The oldest leaves are infected first. Pale greenish-yellow spots, usually less than 1/4 inch, with no definite margins, form on the upper sides of leaves. Olive-green to brown velvety mold forms on the lower leaf surface below leaf spots.

look_alikes.quote: this article will compare Cercospora leaf mold and leaf mold of tomato

conflicts.note: Purdue Vegetable Crops Hotline states 'Leaf mold caused by P. fulva occurs only on leaves,' while UMN Extension states fruit can also be infected in severe cases. The more authoritative UMN Extension source is used as canonical.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Powdery mildew ( Oidium neolycopersici ) of tomato is emerging as an important disease

type_of_disease.quote: In contrast to other fungal plant pathogens, it does not require free water to germinate and cause diseases.

affected_parts.quote: white, powdery sporulation on both the tops and undersides of leaves

summary.value: Light-green to bright yellow lesions appear on leaf surfaces with white powdery coating, eventually forming a dense white layer of growth that can cover entire leaves. Leaves wither and die while remaining attached to the stem.
summary.quote: Symptoms appear on foliage as light-green to bright yellow lesions on the upper leaf surface... A light, powdery coating may be seen on leaf undersides. Under conditions favorable for disease development, a dense, white layewr of growth may develop on both leaf surfaces.

diagnostic_features.value: White powdery sporulation in round spots that begin small but expand and converge, with light-green to bright yellow lesions that become necrotic, and affected leaves withering and dying while remaining attached to the stem. Lesions may exhibit concentric rings.
diagnostic_features.quote: white, powdery sporulation on both the tops and undersides of leaves, in round spots that begin small but expand and converge... light-green to bright yellow lesions on the upper leaf surface. The spots enlarge and become necrotic... Entire leaves wither and die, but remain attached to the stem.

look_alikes.quote: Lesions may exhibit concentric rings similar to early blight.

conflicts.note: UC IPM attributes powdery mildew on field-grown tomatoes to Leveillula taurica, while UMass Extension attributes solanaceous powdery mildew to Oidium neolycopersici. These may represent distinct diseases or distinct pathogens depending on geography and production system. Both are retained; the UMass Extension source is used as canonical for the greenhouse/solanaceous context while the UC IPM record is output separately.

conflicts.canonical_value: Light-green to bright yellow lesions with white powdery coating on both leaf surfaces; leaves wither but remain attached
conflicts.alternative_value: Irregular bright yellow blotches with spots of dead tissue surrounded by yellow halos; abundant white sporulation on upper or lower leaf surfaces; no lesions on stems or fruit
conflicts.note: Symptom description differs between the two powdery mildew pathogens/sources.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: caused by two species of soil-borne fungi- Verticillium dahliae and Verticillium albo-atrum

affected_parts.quote: A yellowing of lower leaves followed by wilting is the first sign of disease. Lesions have a characteristic V-shaped pattern... When the stems of infected plants are cut lengthwise, the vascular tissue exhibits a brown discoloration.

summary.value: Yellowing of lower leaves followed by wilting, with characteristic V-shaped leaf lesions containing brown necrotic tissue surrounded by irregular yellowing.
summary.quote: A yellowing of lower leaves followed by wilting is the first sign of disease. Lesions have a characteristic V-shaped pattern which is widest at the leaf margin. Brown, necrotic tissue within lesions is surrounded by a large, irregular area of yellowing due to a systemic leaf toxin produced by the fungi.

diagnostic_features.value: V-shaped leaf lesions widest at the leaf margin, brown necrotic tissue surrounded by irregular yellowing, brown vascular discoloration visible when stems are cut lengthwise, and one-sided wilting due to asymmetric vascular colonization.
diagnostic_features.quote: Lesions have a characteristic V-shaped pattern which is widest at the leaf margin. Brown, necrotic tissue within lesions is surrounded by a large, irregular area of yellowing... symptoms can appear on one side of the plant or on one side of a leaf because other water-conducting "pipes" remain un-colonized. When the stems of infected plants are cut lengthwise, the vascular tissue exhibits a brown discoloration.

look_alikes.quote: Vascular discoloration and one-sided wilting can also be symptoms of fusarium wilt

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Timber rot (sometime called "white mold") is a stem rot disease that is caused by the fungus Sclerotinia sclerotiorum.

type_of_disease.quote: is a stem rot disease that is caused by the fungus Sclerotinia sclerotiorum

affected_parts.quote: symptoms of timber rot mostly begin as water-soaked areas from the stem axils or in stem joints, either at or above the soil level

summary.value: Water-soaked areas develop on the stem that become covered with white cotton-like mycelium, bleached and hardened, eventually causing wilting, collapse, and plant death.
summary.quote: Symptoms of timber rot mostly begin as water-soaked areas from the stem axils or in stem joints, either at or above the soil level... the stem becomes covered with white "cotton-like" fluffy mycelium and girdled; later, the watersoaked area becomes dry, discolored (bleached appearance) and hard; and the plant (eventually) wilts, collapses, and dies.

diagnostic_features.value: Hard, grayish-black sclerotia about the size of a plump grain of rice embedded within the stem tissue; positive identification achieved by slicing the diseased stem longitudinally.
diagnostic_features.quote: As the disease progresses, hard, grayish-black sclerotia about the size of a plump grain of rice develop... Slicing the diseased stem longitudinally reveals these embedded structures, making positive identification fairly easy.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Rhizopus rot is caused by several species of the genus Rhizopus such as R. stolonifer, R. oryzae, R. arrhizus, and R. microsporus

type_of_disease.quote: The genus Rhizopus comprises cosmopolitan filamentous fungi found in the terrestrial environment

summary.value: Soft, watery, slightly sunken lesions accompanied by progressive growth of whitish-gray mycelia with black sporangia, eventually leading to overall decay of infected commodities.
summary.quote: Rhizopus rot is characterized by soft, watery, slightly sunken lesions accompanied by progressive growth of whitish-gray mycelia with black sporangia. Favorable growth conditions for the pathogen eventually lead to the overall decay of infected commodities

diagnostic_features.value: Soft, watery lesions with whitish-gray mycelia and black sporangia.
diagnostic_features.quote: soft, watery, slightly sunken lesions accompanied by progressive growth of whitish-gray mycelia with black sporangia

conflicts.alternative_value: Rhizopus stolonifer, Rhizopus oryzae, Rhizopus arrhizus
conflicts.note: Source states Rhizopus rot is caused by several species; R. microsporus was the focus of the study but other species are also causal agents.

affected_parts.quote: Ralstonia solanacearum differentially colonizes roots of resistant and susceptible tomato plants; Distribution of Pseudomonas solanacearum in the stem tissues of tomato plants; vascular colonization

look_alikes.quote: it could be cucurbit yellow vine decline, Fusarium, or bacterial wilt that is causing the problem

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Septoria leaf spot is caused by the fungus Septoria lycopersici

type_of_disease.quote: caused by the fungus Septoria lycopersici

affected_parts.quote: Symptoms generally develop on the lower leaves first and then the disease progresses up the plant. Lesions also develop on stems, petioles, and calyx, although fruit are rarely affected.

summary.value: Circular, tan to gray lesions develop on the lower leaves and stems of the plant, typically smaller than 1/8 inch, but can multiply to cause entire leaf blight.
summary.quote: Circular, tan to gray, lesions develop on the lower leaves and stems of the plant. Lesions are typically small (<1/8 in), but as lesions become more numerous the entire leaf may become blighted.

diagnostic_features.value: Small dark spots (pycnidia) in lesion centers where spores are produced; dark-brown perimeter with possible yellow halo; water-soaked appearance on leaf undersides; lesions are smaller than early blight and lack concentric rings; lesion centers do not crack open like gray leaf spot.
diagnostic_features.quote: Small dark spots may appear in the center of the lesion – these are pycnidia, the fruiting body of the fungus where spores are produced. The lesions generally have a dark-brown perimeter and a yellow halo may develop around the leaf lesions. On the underside of the leaves, spots may appear as a darker green color or 'water-soaked.' Lesions caused by the early blight pathogen will be larger and darker brown than Septoria leaf spots and will have concentric rings. Gray leaf spot...will be very similar to Septoria leaf spots where they are small, circular, with a tan or light brown center, but the center part of the lesion tends to crack open or fall out in gray leaf spot lesions.

look_alikes.quote: It can be difficult to distinguish among numerous fungal, foliar leaf spots on tomato. Lesions caused by the early blight pathogen will be larger and darker brown than Septoria leaf spots and will have concentric rings. Gray leaf spot, caused by species of Stemphylium, will be very similar to Septoria leaf spots where they are small, circular, with a tan or light brown center, but the center part of the lesion tends to crack open or fall out in gray leaf spot lesions.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Target spot of tomato, caused by Corynespora cassiicola, was first reported in Florida in 1972.

type_of_disease.quote: In one study, the fungus was isolated from the infested tissues of 39 different plant species

affected_parts.quote: Lesions can form on the roots, stems, and leaves of the plant, but most importantly on the fruits.

summary.value: Leaf lesions are initially dark brown and pinpoint; as they enlarge, centers become light brown to gray with dark outer concentric rings sometimes surrounded by a diffuse yellowing (chlorosis). Fruit lesions start as small, brown, sunken flecks that expand into deeply pitted lesions with characteristic X or star-shaped cracking patterns.
summary.quote: Leaf lesions are initially dark brown and pinpoint... as target spot lesions enlarge, the centers become light brown to gray with dark outer concentric rings sometimes surrounded by a diffuse yellowing (chlorosis)... Fruit lesions start as small, brown, sunken flecks... They often leave a characteristic "X" or star-shaped cracking pattern on badly infested fruit.

diagnostic_features.value: Concentric ring pattern with light brown center and dark outer rings on leaf lesions; deeply pitted fruit lesions that develop during ripening; leaf lesions coalesce to cause blighting and premature defoliation; fruit lesions often develop on the side facing the interior canopy.
diagnostic_features.quote: the centers become light brown to gray with dark outer concentric rings... Those flecks expand into deeply pitted lesions that rapidly develop during ripening... Leaf lesions can develop quickly and coalesce, causing blighting and premature defoliation... Fruit lesions will frequently develop on the side of the fruit facing the interior of the plant canopy

look_alikes.quote: Leaf lesions are initially dark brown and pinpoint, appearing nearly identical to early bacterial spot symptoms caused by Xanthomonas spp... These symptoms are easily confused with those of early blight, caused by Alternaria spp., or those of gray leaf spot, caused by Stemphyllium spp.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Southern blight is caused by the fungus Athelia rolfsii (formerly Sclerotium rolfsii)

type_of_disease.quote: Southern blight is a lethal fungal disease that is most common in the tropics and subtropics.

affected_parts.quote: Southern blight initially leads to a water-soaked appearance on lower leaves or water-soaked lesions (spots) on lower stems. Any plant part that is near or in contact with the soil may become infected. Fruit rots, crown rots and root rots are also typical symptoms of the disease.

summary.value: Initial water-soaked lesions on lower leaves and stems that progress to yellowing and wilting. Infection girdles the base of the stem at the soil line. White fungal mats develop on infected tissue with characteristic spherical resting structures (sclerotia) appearing on infected areas and soil.
summary.quote: Southern blight initially leads to a water-soaked appearance on lower leaves or water-soaked lesions (spots) on lower stems. Infected plants yellow and wilt, often within days of infection, particularly when the weather is moist and warm (80 to 95°F). Thick mats of white fungal threads (called mycelia) may grow from infected tissue, radiating from the plant onto the soil surface. Sclerotia (small spherical structures that are about the size of mustard seeds) develop on infected tissue and on the soil surface.

diagnostic_features.value: Distinctive white fungal mats (mycelia) radiating from infected tissue onto the soil surface, and characteristic spherical sclerotia ranging in color from light tan to dark reddish-brown to black, approximately the size of mustard seeds; white cottony mycelium at the stem base.
diagnostic_features.quote: The Southern blight fungus produces large numbers of spherical, light tan to dark red resting structures called sclerotia. Thick mats of white fungal threads (called mycelia) may grow from infected tissue, radiating from the plant onto the soil surface. Sclerotia range in color from light tan to dark reddish-brown to black.

look_alikes.quote: There have been a few reports of Southern blight ( Sclerotinia rolfsii ) and White mold ( Sclerotinia sclerotiorum ) on tomato and pepper in New Jersey

conflicts.note: Rutgers Plant & Pest Advisory uses Sclerotinia rolfsii; Wisconsin Horticulture extension identifies Athelia rolfsii as the current accepted name with Sclerotium rolfsii as the former name. Sclerotinia rolfsii appears to be an error or alternative synonym used in the Rutgers source.
